test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 11 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Magnetic field lines are always straight lines.
Magnetic field lines start from the south pole and end at the north pole outside the magnet.
Magnetic field is zero at the surface of a current-carrying wire.
The direction of magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor can be given by the right-hand thumb rule.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The direction of magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor can be given by the right-hand thumb rule.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **right-hand thumb rule** is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field generated around a current-carrying conductor. According to this rule, if you hold the conductor with your right hand such that your thumb points in the direction of the current, then the curl of your fingers around the conductor indicates the direction of the magnetic field lines.
 
• **Magnetic field lines are not straight lines.** They are closed continuous curves that emerge from the north pole of a magnet, loop around, and re-enter at the south pole. Hence, the statement that "magnetic field lines are always straight lines" is **incorrect**.
 
• **Magnetic field lines do not start from the south pole and end at the north pole outside the magnet.** They originate from the north pole and terminate at the south pole outside the magnet. Inside the magnet, they travel from the south pole to the north pole, completing a closed loop. Hence, the second statement is **incorrect**.
 
• **Magnetic field is not zero at the surface of a current-carrying wire.** In fact, the magnetic field is strongest at the surface of the conductor and decreases as the distance from the conductor increases. Hence, the third statement is also **incorrect**.
 
• The fourth statement, regarding the **right-hand thumb rule**, is correct as it accurately describes the method to determine the direction of the magnetic field produced by a straight current-carrying conductor.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Right-hand thumb rule:**

 
 
• This rule is specifically applicable to straight current-carrying conductors.
 
• It helps visualize the magnetic field lines in a circular loop around the conductor.
 
• It is an essential concept in electromagnetism, widely used in physics and engineering applications.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic field lines:**
 
 
• These are imaginary lines used to represent the direction and strength of the magnetic field.
 
• The density of the lines indicates the strength of the field; closer lines represent a stronger magnetic field.
 
• They never intersect each other because a magnetic field cannot have two directions at the same point.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic field near a conductor:**
 
 
• The strength of the magnetic field near a current-carrying conductor depends on the current's magnitude and the distance from the conductor.
 
• The magnetic field is proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance (as per Ampere's circuital law).
 
 
 
• **Applications of the right-hand thumb rule:**
 
 
• Used in designing electric motors, generators, and transformers.
 
• Helpful in understanding electromagnetic induction and the behavior of magnetic fields in devices like solenoids and toroids.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Biot-Savart Law:** This law quantifies the magnetic field produced at a point due to a small segment of current-carrying wire.
 
• **Ampere's Circuital Law:** This law relates the integrated magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop.
 
• **Electromagnetic Induction:** The process of generating an electromotive force (EMF) in a conductor due to a changing magnetic field.
 
• **Practical Uses:** The understanding of magnetic fields and their direction is pivotal in developing technologies like MRI machines, electric power transmission systems, and maglev trains.
